visual_accuracy.rationale: Lesson 2 provides conceptually accurate visual representations of the eight flips, combinations, winning cases, and final fraction, whereas Lesson 1 is mathematically mostly correct but relies almost entirely on static text/formula slides with little positional visual depiction of the probability concept.

interactivity.rationale: Both lessons have no available gate specs or plan JSON, so neither demonstrates any functional checkpoints that render questions or accept input.

narration_quality.rationale: Lesson 1 has extremely garbled and unnatural narration with many defects, but Lesson 2 has no available narration at all, making it worse on narration quality because there is no clear, paced audio to evaluate.

sync.rationale: Lesson 1 at least provides narration content, though no beat/timing cues to verify sync, while Lesson 2 provides no transcript or cue data at all, making synchronization entirely unassessable.

concept_accuracy.rationale: Lesson 1 is badly garbled and contains some erroneous statements, but it at least presents the correct binomial setup, counts, and final fraction 93/256, whereas Lesson 2 has no transcript/content available and therefore provides no assessable explanation or learning support.

polish.rationale: Lesson 2 is cleaner and more visually consistent with no visible UI/caption overlays, while Lesson 1, despite more legible slide text, is repeatedly marred by a persistent red cursor, Beamer navigation/footer elements, and subtitles overlapping the bottom of the slides.

aggregator.explanation: The dimension results are mixed, but the confidence-weighted balance slightly favors Lesson 1. Lesson 2 is stronger on visual accuracy and polish, with relatively high confidence, because it presents cleaner visuals and better depictions of the probability cases. However, Lesson 1 wins on narration quality, synchronization, and especially concept accuracy; the concept-accuracy verdict is high-confidence and notes that Lesson 1 at least provides the correct binomial setup and final result, while Lesson 2 lacks assessable explanatory content. Interactivity is a high-confidence tie because neither lesson demonstrates functional checkpoints. Overall, Lesson 1's advantages in assessable instructional substance narrowly outweigh Lesson 2's visual and polish strengths.
